The process is described in the S+ "Guide to Packages"
(spluspackages.pdf).  In a nutshell
   a) from the S+ command line type install.pkgutils()
      to download the required code from our website.
      You should only need to do this once.
   c) install a sufficiently new version of perl (5.8,
      ActiveState recommended on Windows).
   b) set your OS's PATH variable so that the SHOME
      directory and the directories containing the C/C++
      and Fortran compilers and perl are in PATH.
   d) Now use the shell commands
         Splus CMD INSTALL thePackage
      or
         Splus CMD build thePackage
      to install or build it.  (These commands are based
      on what was in R 2.8 or so.  INSTALL is all caps).

messages.subject: Re: GLM problem
messages.body_plain:
It always helps to see a self-contained example of the
problem.  My initial guess was that Ind is a factor variable,
but then you would get nlevels(Ind)-1 coefficients for it
because you have allowed the intercept term in the model.
Perhaps it got read into S+ as a factor because the file it was read
from has some odd characters in it (like '.' for a missing
value).  Use summary() after reading in the data to make
sure it looks like you think it should.  importData has a colTypes
argument to let you force columns to be specific data types
and a na.string argument to let you specify the missing value
string in the file.
 
Also, you said Dep could only have 2 values (1 and 2).  You
might want to make this a factor with those levels so glm()
will do logistic regression.  If Dep is numeric glm() will do
least squares (normal) regression.
 

Bill Dunlap

I suggested groupMeans because he indicated that
speed was important and I suspected that there were
lots of groups.   tapply() is very general but not
as fast as the specialized group* functions:
  > g<-rep(1:1e5, 10) # hundred thousand groups
  > x<-1:1e6          # ten items per group
  > sys.time(v1 <- tapply(x, g, mean))
  [1] 19.391 19.688
  > sys.time(v2 <- groupMeans(x, g))
  [1] 0.516 0.844
  > identical(v1, v2)
  [1] TRUE
S+ also includes groupSums, groupProds, groupMins, groupMaxs,
groupRanges, groupVars, groupStdevs, groupAlls, and groupAnys.

In any case, it is generally faster to work on the data.frame
column by column, applying groupMeans or tapply to the columns
of interest than it is to split the entire data.frame into groups
of rows and then work on the pieces of the data.frame.

messages.body_plain:
I want to use the permutationTest function in the S-Plus resample 
package yield the p-value for a test of zero mean on a data set.  Pretty 
simple stuff, I think. Assume my data set is a vector of length 30 and 
called y. From the documentation, a way to perform the calls is:

permutationTest(data = y, statistic = mean(y)), but permutationTest(y, 
mean) should also work.

However, I get a warning that says "Bootstrap replicates are (nearly) 
identical; does your statistic depend on the resampled data?  In some 
cases bootstrap(..., assign.frame1=T) helps. in: 
makeBootstrap(replicates = reps, observed = observed, n = n, call = 
func.call, seed.start = seed.start,  ...."

When you permute the values in a vector, you get the same elements
in a different order.  The mean is the same.

S+Resample basically supports two kinds of permutation tests:
* tests of a relationship between variables, such as correlation or regression.
  Permute one column of a data set, and keep other columns fixed.
  Recompute the statistic, e.g. correlation.
  Repeat many times, and compare the resampled statistics to the original.
* two-sample tests - pool the data, and randomly divide the pooled data.
  Recompute the statistic, e.g. difference in means.
  Repeat many times, and compare the resampled statistics to the original.

The second case may be viewed as a special case of the first; 
create a two-column dataset, where the first column contains the data
from both samples, and the second column is an indicator of which of
the datasets an observation is from.  Then permute the first column,
keeping the second column fixed.

You cannot perform a permutation test of a single-sample single-variable
statistic, without making some additional assumptions.  For example,
are you willing to assume that if the null hypothesis is true, then
the distribution is symmetric about zero?  If so, you could augment
the data 'x' with '-x', then test the equality of means of the two samples,
by randomly permuting within each pair (S+Resample supports this, look
in the help files for paired or group or stratified).

However, symmetry is a strong assumption.  The biggest problem with
the usual t-test is asymmetry in the population.  Instead 
I'd recommend Johnson's skewness-adjusted t-statistic, JASA 78.
Or a bootstrap BCa or tilting or bootstrap-t confidence interval.

Tim Hesterberg

model2.grp.pval<-as.numeric(nsim)

lp<--0.5+0.65*x1-0.8*x2-0.8*x3+rnorm(size,0,1);

grp<-rbinom(length(lp),1,plogis(lp));

###generate outcome variable###

y<-5.9+1.2*x1-0.9*x2-0.9*x3-0.8*grp+rnorm(size,0,.8)


prop.score<-glm(grp~x1+x2+x3,binomial)$fitted.values


model1<-lm(y~grp+x1+x2+x3)
model1.grp.coeff[i]<-summary(model1)$coefficients[2,1]

model2.grp.coeff[i]<-summary(model2)$coefficients[2,1]
model2.grp.pval[i]<-summary(model2)$coefficients[2,4]


}


mean(model1.grp.coeff)
mean(model2.grp.coeff)

par(mfrow=c(1,2))
hist(model1.grp.coeff)

mean(model1.grp.pval);
median(model1.grp.pval);

The strange thing is model with adjusting covariates x1,x2,x3 has less biased estimates for treatment group (error=abs(-0.8021043+0.8)=0.002)than the model with propensity score adjusted (error=abs(-0.6853582+0.8)=0.115)) on average. the power of 2nd model is also much much lower than the 1st model.

Hello,

I have a fairly large data.frame -- roughly 250k rows by 200 cols.  Most
variables have missing values, many observations have the same variables
missing, same pattern of missingness; there is several of those patterns.

What I would like to get is a list giving me for each missingness pattern
all the indices of the data.frame corresponding to that missingness
pattern.

Using

> na.df <- is.na(data.frame)

I get a logical data.frame giving me the missingness pattern, then

I don't see original.df.  Did you mean to type

A slightly different approach involves splitting
seq(len=nrow(na.df)) by missingness pattern.
To encode the missingness pattern into a character vector
you could do
   missingnessPattern <- do.call("paste", c(list(sep=""), lapply(as.data.frame(na.df), as.integer))
which should map the row
   TRUE TRUE FALSE TRUE
to "1101".  Then use split
   split(seq(len=nrow(na.df), missingNextPattern)

E.g.,
   > d <- data.frame(x=c(1,2,NA,3), y=c(11,12,NA,13), z=c(21,NA,22,23))
   > na.df <- as.data.frame(is.na(d)) #is.na(d) is a matrix, make it a data.frame
   > missingnessPattern <- do.call("paste", c(list(sep=""), lapply(na.df, as.integer)))
   > split(seq(len=nrow(na.df)), missingnessPattern)
   $`000`
   [1] 1 4
   
   $`001`
   [1] 2

   $`110`
   [1] 3

   > d
      x  y  z
   1  1 11 21
   2  2 12 NA
   3 NA NA 22
   4  3 13 23

In R the Reduce function may be able to make that missingnessPattern
using less memory and time (depending on the dataset size) than the
lapply above
   > Reduce(function(a,b)paste(a,as.integer(b),sep=""), x=na.df, init=character(nrow(na.df)))
   [1] "000" "001" "110" "000"
Base S+ does not include the Reduce function.
   
Is that the sort of thing you are looking for?
